cards.title: Name as Highest-Frequency Brand Lever
cards.summary: Treat the brand name as the highest-frequency, longest-lived asset you own, and judge it by whether it creates cumulative strategic advantage rather than by comfort.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much effort and budget to put into naming an ecommerce brand, product line or sub-brand before launch instead of accepting a Friday-afternoon placeholder name.
steps: Reframe the decision: the name is used more often and for longer than any other brand element — every ad, pack, PDP title, email subject line and customer mention repeats it, so an okay name versus the right name compounds over years.

Evaluate candidates against three jobs: (1) get attention in a saturated feed and shelf, (2) hold attention by being processing-fluent — pronounceable and partially understandable, (3) be surprising rather than comfortable or popular.
Ask how the name creates asymmetric advantage for your specific category: does it claim a benefit competitors cannot credibly claim on their own label?

Use the Swiffer versus Ready Mop comparison as the source's illustration, not a benchmark: same floor-cleaning job, Swiffer named to put fun and efficiency into a chore people dislike, Ready Mop described the product they already understood. The source attributes the early gap largely to the name and believes it matters most in the first roughly 12 months of interest, retail listings and press.
Treat that as a presenter's opinion about launch momentum, not a measured causal result.
caveats: Name advantage is stated as most influential in the launch window; after that, marketplace dynamics take over.
Source is a naming-agency creative director speaking from his portfolio; no independent attribution data is presented.

cards.title: Run a Category Audit Before Naming Anything
cards.summary: Map every existing name in the category first so you can define where you will not go, then mine product, consumer need and the ultimate benefit before generating any names.
cards.use_when: Naming a new product, sub-brand or storefront when the category is full of descriptive names (fiber, mop, natural, fresh) and you need a defensible direction rather than a list of words.
steps: Audit the landscape: list the incumbent names and labels in the category. Expect patterns like 'Fiber One', 'Fibre Plus', 'Ready Mop' — descriptive and comfortable. The source's first working hypothesis is usually 'we do not know where we are going, but we know we are not going there.'
Audit your own product: build the list of what is actually different — ingredients, process, format, materials, usage.

Audit the buyer: why do they buy in this category, what do they expect, and what is the ultimate benefit up the ladder from the functional one? For a cleaning tool the ultimate benefit included less drudgery; the source found people happily polish furniture or wash windows but nobody wants to mop.

Ask the four sequence questions: How do you define winning here? What do you have to win (real product facts)? What do you need to win (the breakthrough claim)? What do we need to say? Different stakeholders answer 'winning' differently — surface that before creating.
Only then articulate a naming strategy, and accept that a name cannot carry everything: packaging, copy and go-to-market carry the rest.
Ecommerce application: this audit doubles as your PDP positioning brief — the ultimate benefit you uncover becomes the hero claim, not the ingredient list.
caveats: You may return to a rejected direction once the product truth is clearer; the first hypothesis is a starting filter, not a verdict.
For ordinary commodity products without a breakthrough feature, the differentiation often has to come from the benefit framing rather than a unique ingredient.

cards.title: Name the Ultimate Benefit, Not the Product Category
cards.summary: Move the brand away from describing the category and toward the emotional or functional endpoint the buyer actually wants.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP hero copy, naming a new SKU, or repositioning a supplement, food or personal-care product where every competitor's label says the same category word.
steps: Observe that most category labels assume buyers already know the category is good for them — the source's example: every fiber package says 'fiber' and stops there.
Climb the benefit ladder with real customer language: gut health, regularity, metabolism, digestion, feeling lighter.

Watch physical reactions as much as words — in the source's exercise, a posture shift and an upward hand motion produced 'you feel lighter' as the real territory, and the naming director latched onto it.

Build the naming territory from that endpoint rather than the ingredient. From 'light' the source's hunting grounds included Greek and Latin roots for light, expressions about feeling light, aerodynamics and how a wing generates lift.

Check the resulting name against shelf reality: the example was a new fiber brand called 'Feather' sitting between 'Fiber Plus' and Metamucil, plus a supporting line such as a lightweight fiber, with 'fiber' still present on the label so shoppers are not confused.
Ecommerce translation: put the category word in metadata, filters and secondary copy for search, and put the benefit word in the brand name and hero headline.
Keep the claim honest — the name can lead the benefit, but the product has to deliver it.
caveats: The Feather example is an in-conversation thought exercise, not a launched brand with results.
Forcing an abstract benefit name onto a highly search-driven commodity category can hurt discoverability unless the category term stays visible in titles and tags.

cards.title: Quantity Leads to Quality: Generate Roughly 2,000 Names
cards.summary: Commit to large-volume generation with deliberate permission to produce bad ideas, because the source treats a 50-100 name list as the point where teams wrongly stop.
cards.use_when: Running any divergent naming, campaign or creative sprint for a store, SKU or ad concept and tempted to converge after the first hundred ideas.
steps: Set the volume expectation explicitly: the source said clients often come back stuck with 50-100 names, while his team works toward roughly 2,000 candidate words written down. These are not 2,000 good names — most are raw material he internally calls 'trash'.

Separate generation from evaluation in time: run a divergent cycle, then a second cycle, then start cutting. The source's cycle is roughly two rounds over about two to two and a half weeks, with team members also working on other projects.
After the divergence, return to the creative framework and objectives and ask whether each angle produced anything usable before shipping a shortlist to legal.
Apply to ecommerce creative broadly: the same volume logic holds for ad hooks, PDP headline variants and email subject lines, where the good ones are usually found by writing many bad ones first.
Budget volume against your clock — the source can pursue this because names are his core product; a small operator should scale the number down but keep the ratio of generation to selection.
caveats: 2,000 is the source agency's working number for a paid naming engagement, not a required target for every creative task.
Volume without an explicit selection framework just produces a longer unusable list.

cards.title: Replace Brainstorming With Small Teams and Shifting Briefs
cards.summary: Abandon group brainstorming; run two-person teams on deliberately different briefs so the candidate pool contains genuinely distinct naming directions.
cards.use_when: Structuring an internal or agency naming/creative sprint for a new brand, SKU or campaign and deciding how many people should work on it and with what information.
steps: Drop the large brainstorm: the source cites peer pressure in groups and the difficulty of stopping the group's evaluation cascade with four, six or ten people, plus a slow grind. He ran an internal study across roughly 18 months and concluded his best names came from individuals or two-person teams, not freelancers or brainstorm sessions.

Split into small teams with different information diets. In the source's fiber example: Team 1 knows everything about the product; Team 2 knows it is fiber plus an added energy or mineral ingredient; Team 3 is not briefed on fiber at all and works on athletic performance. The third brief produces names the first two would never reach.
Expect three distinct lists rather than one blended list, and keep them separate so you can see which framing generates the energy.
Give teams explicit permission to fail — the source states that if the team is not failing, it is not doing the job. Treat the raw output as a treasure hunt rather than a deliverable.

Ecommerce adaptation: in a small store, simulate this by running the same naming or PDP-copy brief through three different lenses — product specs, buyer outcome, and an unrelated domain (aviation, sport, hometown street names) — rather than three people.
caveats: The 18-month internal study is the source's private research; methodology is described as 'a little sloppy and crude' by his own account.
Two-person teams assume availability; solo operators should substitute sequential briefs, not skip the diversity of framing.

cards.title: Systematic Treasure-Hunt Databases for Naming
cards.summary: Mine enriched reference databases — roots, mythologies, the periodic table, plus your own cross-category archive — instead of waiting for inspiration.
cards.use_when: Filling the candidate pool for a new brand or product name when the obvious descriptive options are taken or legally blocked.
steps: Work from commonly available sources first: Latin roots, Greek roots, Roman and Greek mythology. The source cites Intel Pentium as an output of periodic-table work.

Enrich the source rather than using it raw: the agency loads the periodic table with additional articles and vocabulary so the word pool around each element is much larger than the bare table — that extra layer is where the good candidates appear.

Build a cross-category archive: the source files names by theme, not by product. A small car for Nissan and a small Intel processor both go into a database called 'small things', so unrelated assignments feed each other.
Assign short, bounded side hunts inside a naming project — for the 'light' territory the source had someone spend about 15 minutes on what makes an airplane lift.

Embrace synchronicity: the source describes connecting seemingly irrelevant things as the fundamental layer of creativity, illustrated by Impossible Burger refusing to sound like a natural-foods product that would blend into Whole Foods.

Ecommerce application: when naming a supplement, subscription box or private-label SKU, run 20-30 minute side hunts into an unrelated domain (aviation, geology, street names, sports) and look for transferable words rather than direct category synonyms.
caveats: Databases are a starting point, not a source of finished names; raw output needs heavy filtering.
Watch for trademark collisions — the source routes shortlists through paralegals and trademark attorneys before presentation.

cards.title: Run a 20-Minute Personal Naming Session
cards.summary: Use a repeatable solo routine — free-associate on paper, ask AI for context rather than names, then chase promising directions into actual candidates.
cards.use_when: Sitting down to generate names or headline options yourself for a product, bundle or campaign and needing to get into flow quickly.
steps: Start with a pad and pen and free-associate about the direction before touching a screen; the source sometimes draws a treasure-map grid and places ideas in it.

Do not ask AI tools for names. Ask them questions about the subject matter — for a fiber product, questions about fiber, digestion, lightness — and use the answers to seed directions. Verify any tool's current interface and capability, since these change.
Pick a promising territory, e.g. Greek words for light, aviation and lift, other words for light leading to sunshine and soil, and then start crafting actual candidate names.
Keep the whole session short: the source describes this as roughly a 20-minute activity, not an arduous process — the point is starting to move, not completing the job in one sitting.
Treat the paper notes as the raw dump and the crafted names as the output; expect a long session-free interval is not required for solo generation.
Ecommerce application: run this before writing PDP titles, bundle names or campaign hooks, and keep the resulting direction notes as a tagged file you can revisit for future SKUs.
caveats: This routine reflects one practitioner's working method, not a validated protocol.
Using AI for context rather than name generation is the source's stated approach; his competitive claim now rests on judging names from proprietary data.

cards.title: Separate Divergence From Evaluation and Reframe Rejections
cards.summary: Protect the creative phase by replacing immediate rejection with problem-posing language, and delay real evaluation until later cycles.
cards.use_when: Reviewing creative submissions from staff or agencies — naming options, ad concepts, PDP concepts — and catching yourself about to kill an idea in the room.
steps: Adopt the source's two stock phrases when an idea triggers a 'no': replace 'that's too expensive' with 'I wish we could make that so it wasn't expensive', and replace 'that'll never pass legal' with 'how do we modify that so it's legally available?' Both convert rejection into a solvable problem, which the source says humans are wired to want to solve.
Use softer openers first: 'that's interesting' or the source's preferred 'I wouldn't have thought of that' — framed as honest credit-giving rather than faint praise.

Model the behavior visibly: the source, as creative director, says his team knows he will speculate on their list rather than evaluate it harshly. If you are the founder reviewing your own staff's work, that visible restraint is what gives them courage — the source roots 'encouragement' in 'courage'.
Delay the cutover: give ideas a period where they simply live in the system, then start pairing down. In the agency process trademark review also automatically prunes candidates.

When you do switch to converging, do it deliberately after about two cycles, revisit the objectives and creative framework, and treat the framework as a window for creation rather than a set of five conformity boxes.
Ecommerce application: apply this to ad-hook and landing-page headline review so early concepts are not killed by the person with the loudest veto before any traffic test.
caveats: Permission to speculate does not remove eventual client or business evaluation; the source explicitly says people still have to do the right thing for clients.
Soft language only works if the underlying idea later gets a genuine decision — constant deferral stalls the project.

cards.title: The Comfort Trap: Polarizing Names Carry Energy
cards.summary: Judge an idea by whether it sits in a high-energy tension zone or the invisible consensus zone, and treat strong internal polarization as a signal rather than a defect.
cards.use_when: Deciding between a safe, easily-approved brand name, campaign concept or offer angle and a polarizing one that some of your team dislikes.
steps: Draw the two zones: the tension zone, where roughly half the team resists the idea, energy is high and the choice is polarizing; and the invisible zone, where consensus is high, the choice feels safe, and distinctiveness is near zero.

Expect comfortable names to test well in research precisely because they merely confirm the category — the source's example is Clorox's Ready Mop reading as a mop that respondents understood immediately.

When an idea polarizes internally, do not discard it automatically. The source's version of this insight came from Andy Grove reviewing Intel's Pentium, who argued a good name is so polarizing that it carries energy — and the source's advice is to examine what inside the word is creating that energy even if you ultimately do not use it.
Apply the test to ecommerce inputs: a product name, a bundle framing, a founder-led ad concept or a bold hero claim. Ask whether it produces an internal reaction or glides by.

Pair this with believability: before presenting polarizing candidates, the source's team applies one rule internally — is that believable? The first sub-second reaction must lean toward 'I believe this could exist'.
Use a context mock-up (see separate card on proof of concept) to test believability before showing the client or publishing.
caveats: Polarization is a signal of energy, not proof of quality — the source says you may not decide to use it.
Believability at first glance is a stated agency rule, not a published benchmark.

cards.title: Present Names in Context, Not as a Spreadsheet
cards.summary: Show naming candidates inside realistic artifacts — press headlines, sponsored placements, product mock-ups — so decision-makers can feel how the name performs.
cards.use_when: Presenting name or brand options to founders, retailers or internal stakeholders who rarely make creative decisions and are choosing between unfamiliar candidates.
steps: Build a 'proof of concept' for two or three finalists before anyone outside the team sees them. Internally the source's team applies one test: does this look believable in context?

Place the name in realistic settings: a Wall Street Journal-style article layout, an endorsement ad with a famous actor or tennis player in a black-and-white photograph and a line like companies that run well run on [name], or on merchandise and transit creative.

Use the mock-up to test whether the candidate survives first-glance processing — in under a second the viewer should lean toward believing the thing could actually exist. The example given is Microsoft Azure: believable as a cloud brand even though Microsoft's portfolio is typically descriptive.
Recognize the psychological reason: most decision-makers have little practice making creative decisions, so context supplies the comparison that a plain list cannot.
For a store, the equivalent artifacts are a mocked PDP header, an ad in a familiar placement, a packaging visual, or a search results listing — show the name where customers will actually meet it.
Keep the set small: the source presents roughly 10, sometimes 15 names in a list, but tests believability internally on a narrower finalist set first.
caveats: Context presentation influences perception and can sway stakeholders — it is a decision aid, not consumer evidence.
Mock-ups must not imply real coverage or real endorsements that do not exist.

cards.title: Score Nameless Knowledge: Judging Names You Did Not Create
cards.summary: Evaluate names by expectedness relative to the owner, sound symbolism and familiarity-plus-surprise, rather than by personal taste.
cards.use_when: Choosing between shortlisted names for a brand, collection or product line and needing a consistent scoring rationale rather than gut preference.
steps: Use the source's rule for scoring: no sevens. Force a strong call rather than a lukewarm middle score, because middling marks hide the specific quality that makes a name work.

Ask whether the name is unexpected for this particular company: the source rated Microsoft Azure highly because Azure is an outlier in a portfolio of descriptive names, and noted the same name would be less surprising from Google.

Check processing fluency: can a person pronounce it, and is there something understandable inside it? The source describes the target as surprisingly familiar, because brains are lazy but still need an interesting hook.

Consider sound symbolism: consonant-vowel-consonant-vowel structure is what children first learn, and letters have perceived speed — in the source's framework P, K, B sounds read as reliable and fast, with D, P and Z reading fast, and the letter X signaling innovation in tech and cars.
Check multi-market legibility, since names are often shipped across several markets; the source tested Blackberry in roughly six countries and languages, but note that testing was expensive.

Apply to ecommerce: score brand and collection names by how predictable they are for your category (Fiber One, Natural Farms), whether the word is easy to say aloud in a video ad, and whether it survives being heard once rather than seen.
caveats: The 1-10 scores are the source's subjective creative judgment, made without knowing the companies.
Sound-symbolism claims are presented as the agency's accumulated research; they are directional, not guarantees of consumer response.
The naming mechanics of specific sound symbolism belong to brand-creative work rather than store operations.

cards.title: When to Rename and How to Launch It
cards.summary: The source's rule: names compound, so get it right early; when you do rename, lead with enthusiasm and a clear story rather than fear of losing equity.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to change a store, product line or brand name that creates friction in search, spelling or customer recall, and planning the relaunch.
steps: Start from the compounding premise: the longer a name sits in the market the more advantage it accumulates through familiarity, which is the source's argument for getting naming right at the very beginning instead of a Friday-afternoon session.

Identify friction as the trigger: the source says bad names simply create friction. His cited example was Kodium, which no one knew or could spell and which had poor search performance, renamed to Windsurf over about a six-week period — the source attributes the brand's takeoff partly to the name. Treat that as the source's example, not a guaranteed outcome.

Check for the simple cases first: being sued is a straightforward reason to rename. Otherwise, work through pluses and minuses and decline the project if the owner is determined to keep the old name at all costs.
Target young companies: the source says for a Series A or B company a rename is not traumatic, whereas for a Coca-Cola-scale business you need a compelling reason.

Counter the standard objection with the source's claim: the biggest reason people refuse to rename is fear of losing equity and momentum, and he states he has never seen that loss materialize, provided the launch is done with enthusiasm and a story — 'we were here, now we're going this way, and here is the benefit to you'. Customers know the software and technology have not changed.
Use the removal of friction as the payoff over the following six to nine months of extra invested resources.

For a store: migration means new domain or brand assets, redirects, updated marketplace listings, and a customer-facing announcement that leads with what stays the same (products, team, quality) and what improves.
caveats: The 'never seen equity loss' claim is the source's agency experience, not independent research.
Consumer-goods giants with decades of brand equity are explicitly excluded from the easy-rename advice.
Renaming carries real SEO, marketplace-listing and repeat-purchase risk that the source does not quantify.

cards.title: Apply a Creative Curiosity Process
cards.summary: Operate naming and positioning work as a repeatable combination of category audit, product and consumer research, four strategy questions, then generation — not as one burst of inspiration.
cards.use_when: Setting up the brief for naming, positioning or a major PDP rewrite, or diagnosing why your creative output keeps landing in the invisible zone.
steps: Step 1 — landscape: list what exists in the category and form a first hypothesis about what you are not going to be.
Step 2 — product: build the factual list of what your product actually has and does.
Step 3 — consumer: establish why they buy, what they expect, and the ultimate benefit up the ladder.

Step 4 — strategy questions, which the source says pay off greatly with almost no exceptions: How do you define winning? What do you have to win? What do you need to win? What do we need to say? Expect six stakeholders to give different answers to the winning question.
Step 5 — generate in small teams or solo, working across several unusual directions, with permission to fail and a target of large volume.
Step 6 — converge after roughly two cycles against the creative framework, prune legally, and narrow to about 10-15 candidates.
Step 7 — test believability and the sound-fluency properties, then present in context.
For ecommerce, steps 2 and 3 come from your own product specs plus reviews, support tickets and search queries rather than agency interviews — the inputs differ, the sequence does not.
caveats: The full agency process takes weeks and multiple people; small operators must compress it without skipping the sequencing.
Timing bands such as two cycles in two and a half weeks assume team members working several projects at once.

cards.title: Discipline, Not Talent: Managing Creative Contributors
cards.summary: Treat creativity as an acquired skill built through persistent process, and manage contributors by removing evaluation fear rather than by demanding brilliance.
cards.use_when: Founders or operators trying to scale creative output beyond themselves for naming, ad creative, PDP copy or content.
steps: Reframe the belief: the source, whose process is highly systematized, describes creativity as process-driven and therefore teachable, not as raw talent — Leonardo da Vinci's method is cited as persistence and tenacity rather than a single burst.

Change how you respond to submissions: the source's rule as creative director is to speculate on a list rather than evaluate it, and his team knows that. If people get smacked down on their first bad idea, they stop producing useful ideas.
Notice what encouragement means literally — the source points out its root is courage, and asks whether you are actually giving people room to flow rather than leading every move.
Watch the difference between leading and managing, and between evaluating and encouraging, as the source's diagnosis of the habitual management mistake.

Protect the generation phase from judgment by structure, not willpower: separate the dreaming, planning and judging stages the way Disney's three-room practice is described, so judgment happens at a scheduled point rather than in the moment of ideation.
Invite the person who produced the rejected idea to solve the constraint (cost, legal availability) rather than dropping the idea.
caveats: These are the source's management prescriptions and personal practice, not measured team-performance results.
Small teams may not be able to isolate phases in separate people; they still need to isolate them in time.

cards.title: Use an Inconvenient Outside Source to Force New Connections
cards.summary: Spend 30 minutes in unfamiliar material and deliberately look for transferable connections before finalizing creative work.
cards.use_when: A headline, PDP narrative, campaign angle or product story feels like generic category copy and you need a genuinely different perspective.
steps: Choose genuinely unfamiliar material for the category — a couple of magazines you never read, or a book on a subject unrelated to your product such as Thomas Edison.
Spend about 30 minutes reading only for connections that could move into the piece, suspending logic and evaluation during that window.
The source's claim, from his own practice, is that roughly 30% of the time this yields a new perspective, spin or insight for the work — treat that as his experience, not a measured rate.

This supports the source's broader principle of synchronicity: creativity comes from connecting seemingly irrelevant things. Impossible Burger is the cited case — deliberately not a natural-foods-style name that would blend into the Whole Foods shelf.

Extend the same move to the natural world, which the source sometimes uses as a direct source: for 'lightness' he looked at what makes an airplane lift, and at Greek roots and expressions for feeling light.

Ecommerce application: before finalizing a product narrative or ad hook, read one industry-adjacent and one completely unrelated publication or community, and mine them for a metaphor or angle you can justify with your real product facts.
Make the borrowed angle serve the product truth, not replace it — a clever reference that overstates the product breaks believability.
caveats: The 30% hit rate is the source's own estimate from practice.
Borrowed metaphors must be checked against what your product actually does before use in claims.

Treat the raw output as a treasure hunt rather than a deliverable.","Ecommerce adaptation: in a small store, simulate this by running the same naming or PDP-copy brief through three different lenses — product specs, buyer outcome, and an unrelated domain (aviation, sport, hometown street names) — rather than three people."],"caveats":["The 18-month internal study is the source's private research; methodology is described as 'a little sloppy and crude' by his own account.","Two-person teams assume availability; solo operators should substitute sequential briefs, not skip the diversity of framing."],"tags":["brand","naming","creative-strategy","ideation","process","team-management"]},{"title":"Systematic Treasure-Hunt Databases for Naming","summary":"Mine enriched reference databases — roots, mythologies, the periodic table, plus your own cross-category archive — instead of waiting for inspiration.","use_when":"Filling the candidate pool for a new brand or product name when the obvious descriptive options are taken or legally blocked.","steps":["Work from commonly available sources first: Latin roots, Greek roots, Roman and Greek mythology. The source cites Intel Pentium as an output of periodic-table work.","Enrich the source rather than using it raw: the agency loads the periodic table with additional articles and vocabulary so the word pool around each element is much larger than the bare table — that extra layer is where the good candidates appear.","Build a cross-category archive: the source files names by theme, not by product. A small car for Nissan and a small Intel processor both go into a database called 'small things', so unrelated assignments feed each other.","Assign short, bounded side hunts inside a naming project — for the 'light' territory the source had someone spend about 15 minutes on what makes an airplane lift.","Embrace synchronicity: the source describes connecting seemingly irrelevant things as the fundamental layer of creativity, illustrated by Impossible Burger refusing to sound like a natural-foods product that would blend into Whole Foods.","Ecommerce application: when naming a supplement, subscription box or private-label SKU, run 20-30 minute side hunts into an unrelated domain (aviation, geology, street names, sports) and look for transferable words rather than direct category synonyms."],"caveats":["Databases are a starting point, not a source of finished names; raw output needs heavy filtering.","Watch for trademark collisions — the source routes shortlists through paralegals and trademark attorneys before presentation."],"tags":["brand","naming","creative-strategy","research","ideation","differentiation"]},{"title":"Run a 20-Minute Personal Naming Session","summary":"Use a repeatable solo routine — free-associate on paper, ask AI for context rather than names, then chase promising directions into actual candidates.","use_when":"Sitting down to generate names or headline options yourself for a product, bundle or campaign and needing to get into flow quickly.","steps":["Start with a pad and pen and free-associate about the direction before touching a screen; the source sometimes draws a treasure-map grid and places ideas in it.","Do not ask AI tools for names. Ask them questions about the subject matter — for a fiber product, questions about fiber, digestion, lightness — and use the answers to seed directions. Verify any tool's current interface and capability, since these change.","Pick a promising territory, e.g. Greek words for light, aviation and lift, other words for light leading to sunshine and soil, and then start crafting actual candidate names.","Keep the whole session short: the source describes this as roughly a 20-minute activity, not an arduous process — the point is starting to move, not completing the job in one sitting.","Treat the paper notes as the raw dump and the crafted names as the output; expect a long session-free interval is not required for solo generation.","Ecommerce application: run this before writing PDP titles, bundle names or campaign hooks, and keep the resulting direction notes as a tagged file you can revisit for future SKUs."],"caveats":["This routine reflects one practitioner's working method, not a validated protocol.","Using AI for context rather than name generation is the source's stated approach; his competitive claim now rests on judging names from proprietary data."],"tags":["brand","naming","creative-strategy","ideation","ai-tools","process"]},{"title":"Separate Divergence From Evaluation and Reframe Rejections","summary":"Protect the creative phase by replacing immediate rejection with problem-posing language, and delay real evaluation until later cycles.","use_when":"Reviewing creative submissions from staff or agencies — naming options, ad concepts, PDP concepts — and catching yourself about to kill an idea in the room.","steps":["Adopt the source's two stock phrases when an idea triggers a 'no': replace 'that's too expensive' with 'I wish we could make that so it wasn't expensive', and replace 'that'll never pass legal' with 'how do we modify that so it's legally available?' Both convert rejection into a solvable problem, which the source says humans are wired to want to solve.","Use softer openers first: 'that's interesting' or the source's preferred 'I wouldn't have thought of that' — framed as honest credit-giving rather than faint praise.","Model the behavior visibly: the source, as creative director, says his team knows he will speculate on their list rather than evaluate it harshly. If you are the founder reviewing your own staff's work, that visible restraint is what gives them courage — the source roots 'encouragement' in 'courage'.","Delay the cutover: give ideas a period where they simply live in the system, then start pairing down. In the agency process trademark review also automatically prunes candidates.","When you do switch to converging, do it deliberately after about two cycles, revisit the objectives and creative framework, and treat the framework as a window for creation rather than a set of five conformity boxes.","Ecommerce application: apply this to ad-hook and landing-page headline review so early concepts are not killed by the person with the loudest veto before any traffic test."],"caveats":["Permission to speculate does not remove eventual client or business evaluation; the source explicitly says people still have to do the right thing for clients.","Soft language only works if the underlying idea later gets a genuine decision — constant deferral stalls the project."],"tags":["creative-strategy","ideation","team-management","naming","experiment-design","process"]},{"title":"The Comfort Trap: Polarizing Names Carry Energy","summary":"Judge an idea by whether it sits in a high-energy tension zone or the invisible consensus zone, and treat strong internal polarization as a signal rather than a defect.","use_when":"Deciding between a safe, easily-approved brand name, campaign concept or offer angle and a polarizing one that some of your team dislikes.","steps":["Draw the two zones: the tension zone, where roughly half the team resists the idea, energy is high and the choice is polarizing; and the invisible zone, where consensus is high, the choice feels safe, and distinctiveness is near zero.","Expect comfortable names to test well in research precisely because they merely confirm the category — the source's example is Clorox's Ready Mop reading as a mop that respondents understood immediately.","When an idea polarizes internally, do not discard it automatically. The source's version of this insight came from Andy Grove reviewing Intel's Pentium, who argued a good name is so polarizing that it carries energy — and the source's advice is to examine what inside the word is creating that energy even if you ultimately do not use it.","Apply the test to ecommerce inputs: a product name, a bundle framing, a founder-led ad concept or a bold hero claim. Ask whether it produces an internal reaction or glides by.","Pair this with believability: before presenting polarizing candidates, the source's team applies one rule internally — is that believable? The first sub-second reaction must lean toward 'I believe this could exist'.","Use a context mock-up (see separate card on proof of concept) to test believability before showing the client or publishing."],"caveats":["Polarization is a signal of energy, not proof of quality — the source says you may not decide to use it.","Believability at first glance is a stated agency rule, not a published benchmark."],"tags":["brand","naming","differentiation","positioning","creative-strategy","conversion-optimization"]},{"title":"Present Names in Context, Not as a Spreadsheet","summary":"Show naming candidates inside realistic artifacts — press headlines, sponsored placements, product mock-ups — so decision-makers can feel how the name performs.","use_when":"Presenting name or brand options to founders, retailers or internal stakeholders who rarely make creative decisions and are choosing between unfamiliar candidates.","steps":["Build a 'proof of concept' for two or three finalists before anyone outside the team sees them. Internally the source's team applies one test: does this look believable in context?","Place the name in realistic settings: a Wall Street Journal-style article layout, an endorsement ad with a famous actor or tennis player in a black-and-white photograph and a line like companies that run well run on [name], or on merchandise and transit creative.","Use the mock-up to test whether the candidate survives first-glance processing — in under a second the viewer should lean toward believing the thing could actually exist. The example given is Microsoft Azure: believable as a cloud brand even though Microsoft's portfolio is typically descriptive.","Recognize the psychological reason: most decision-makers have little practice making creative decisions, so context supplies the comparison that a plain list cannot.","For a store, the equivalent artifacts are a mocked PDP header, an ad in a familiar placement, a packaging visual, or a search results listing — show the name where customers will actually meet it.","Keep the set small: the source presents roughly 10, sometimes 15 names in a list, but tests believability internally on a narrower finalist set first."],"caveats":["Context presentation influences perception and can sway stakeholders — it is a decision aid, not consumer evidence.","Mock-ups must not imply real coverage or real endorsements that do not exist."],"tags":["brand","naming","positioning","landing-page","creative-strategy","merchandising","stakeholder-management"]},{"title":"Score Nameless Knowledge: Judging Names You Did Not Create","summary":"Evaluate names by expectedness relative to the owner, sound symbolism and familiarity-plus-surprise, rather than by personal taste.","use_when":"Choosing between shortlisted names for a brand, collection or product line and needing a consistent scoring rationale rather than gut preference.","steps":["Use the source's rule for scoring: no sevens. Force a strong call rather than a lukewarm middle score, because middling marks hide the specific quality that makes a name work.","Ask whether the name is unexpected for this particular company: the source rated Microsoft Azure highly because Azure is an outlier in a portfolio of descriptive names, and noted the same name would be less surprising from Google.","Check processing fluency: can a person pronounce it, and is there something understandable inside it? The source describes the target as surprisingly familiar, because brains are lazy but still need an interesting hook.","Consider sound symbolism: consonant-vowel-consonant-vowel structure is what children first learn, and letters have perceived speed — in the source's framework P, K, B sounds read as reliable and fast, with D, P and Z reading fast, and the letter X signaling innovation in tech and cars.","Check multi-market legibility, since names are often shipped across several markets; the source tested Blackberry in roughly six countries and languages, but note that testing was expensive.","Apply to ecommerce: score brand and collection names by how predictable they are for your category (Fiber One, Natural Farms), whether the word is easy to say aloud in a video ad, and whether it survives being heard once rather than seen."],"caveats":["The 1-10 scores are the source's subjective creative judgment, made without knowing the companies.","Sound-symbolism claims are presented as the agency's accumulated research; they are directional, not guarantees of consumer response.","The naming mechanics of specific sound symbolism belong to brand-creative work rather than store operations."],"tags":["brand","naming","differentiation","creative-strategy","ad-creative","measurement"]},{"title":"When to Rename and How to Launch It","summary":"The source's rule: names compound, so get it right early; when you do rename, lead with enthusiasm and a clear story rather than fear of losing equity.","use_when":"Deciding whether to change a store, product line or brand name that creates friction in search, spelling or customer recall, and planning the relaunch.","steps":["Start from the compounding premise: the longer a name sits in the market the more advantage it accumulates through familiarity, which is the source's argument for getting naming right at the very beginning instead of a Friday-afternoon session.","Identify friction as the trigger: the source says bad names simply create friction. His cited example was Kodium, which no one knew or could spell and which had poor search performance, renamed to Windsurf over about a six-week period — the source attributes the brand's takeoff partly to the name. Treat that as the source's example, not a guaranteed outcome.","Check for the simple cases first: being sued is a straightforward reason to rename. Otherwise, work through pluses and minuses and decline the project if the owner is determined to keep the old name at all costs.","Target young companies: the source says for a Series A or B company a rename is not traumatic, whereas for a Coca-Cola-scale business you need a compelling reason.","Counter the standard objection with the source's claim: the biggest reason people refuse to rename is fear of losing equity and momentum, and he states he has never seen that loss materialize, provided the launch is done with enthusiasm and a story — 'we were here, now we're going this way, and here is the benefit to you'. Customers know the software and technology have not changed.","Use the removal of friction as the payoff over the following six to nine months of extra invested resources.","For a store: migration means new domain or brand assets, redirects, updated marketplace listings, and a customer-facing announcement that leads with what stays the same (products, team, quality) and what improves."],"caveats":["The 'never seen equity loss' claim is the source's agency experience, not independent research.","Consumer-goods giants with decades of brand equity are explicitly excluded from the easy-rename advice.","Renaming carries real SEO, marketplace-listing and repeat-purchase risk that the source does not quantify."],"tags":["brand","naming","positioning","retention","search","acquisition","process"]},{"title":"Apply a Creative Curiosity Process","summary":"Operate naming and positioning work as a repeatable combination of category audit, product and consumer research, four strategy questions, then generation — not as one burst of inspiration.","use_when":"Setting up the brief for naming, positioning or a major PDP rewrite, or diagnosing why your creative output keeps landing in the invisible zone.","steps":["Step 1 — landscape: list what exists in the category and form a first hypothesis about what you are not going to be.","Step 2 — product: build the factual list of what your product actually has and does.","Step 3 — consumer: establish why they buy, what they expect, and the ultimate benefit up the ladder.","Step 4 — strategy questions, which the source says pay off greatly with almost no exceptions: How do you define winning? What do you have to win? What do you need to win? What do we need to say? Expect six stakeholders to give different answers to the winning question.","Step 5 — generate in small teams or solo, working across several unusual directions, with permission to fail and a target of large volume.","Step 6 — converge after roughly two cycles against the creative framework, prune legally, and narrow to about 10-15 candidates.","Step 7 — test believability and the sound-fluency properties, then present in context.","For ecommerce, steps 2 and 3 come from your own product specs plus reviews, support tickets and search queries rather than agency interviews — the inputs differ, the sequence does not."],"caveats":["The full agency process takes weeks and multiple people; small operators must compress it without skipping the sequencing.","Timing bands such as two cycles in two and a half weeks assume team members working several projects at once."],"tags":["brand","naming","positioning","process","customer-research","creative-strategy","product-page"]},{"title":"Discipline, Not Talent: Managing Creative Contributors","summary":"Treat creativity as an acquired skill built through persistent process, and manage contributors by removing evaluation fear rather than by demanding brilliance.","use_when":"Founders or operators trying to scale creative output beyond themselves for naming, ad creative, PDP copy or content.","steps":["Reframe the belief: the source, whose process is highly systematized, describes creativity as process-driven and therefore teachable, not as raw talent — Leonardo da Vinci's method is cited as persistence and tenacity rather than a single burst.","Change how you respond to submissions: the source's rule as creative director is to speculate on a list rather than evaluate it, and his team knows that. If people get smacked down on their first bad idea, they stop producing useful ideas.","Notice what encouragement means literally — the source points out its root is courage, and asks whether you are actually giving people room to flow rather than leading every move.","Watch the difference between leading and managing, and between evaluating and encouraging, as the source's diagnosis of the habitual management mistake.","Protect the generation phase from judgment by structure, not willpower: separate the dreaming, planning and judging stages the way Disney's three-room practice is described, so judgment happens at a scheduled point rather than in the moment of ideation.","Invite the person who produced the rejected idea to solve the constraint (cost, legal availability) rather than dropping the idea."],"caveats":["These are the source's management prescriptions and personal practice, not measured team-performance results.","Small teams may not be able to isolate phases in separate people; they still need to isolate them in time."],"tags":["team-management","creative-strategy","ideation","process","leadership","content"]},{"title":"Use an Inconvenient Outside Source to Force New Connections","summary":"Spend 30 minutes in unfamiliar material and deliberately look for transferable connections before finalizing creative work.","use_when":"A headline, PDP narrative, campaign angle or product story feels like generic category copy and you need a genuinely different perspective.","steps":["Choose genuinely unfamiliar material for the category — a couple of magazines you never read, or a book on a subject unrelated to your product such as Thomas Edison.","Spend about 30 minutes reading only for connections that could move into the piece, suspending logic and evaluation during that window.","The source's claim, from his own practice, is that roughly 30% of the time this yields a new perspective, spin or insight for the work — treat that as his experience, not a measured rate.","This supports the source's broader principle of synchronicity: creativity comes from connecting seemingly irrelevant things. Impossible Burger is the cited case — deliberately not a natural-foods-style name that would blend into the Whole Foods shelf.","Extend the same move to the natural world, which the source sometimes uses as a direct source: for 'lightness' he looked at what makes an airplane lift, and at Greek roots and expressions for feeling light.","Ecommerce application: before finalizing a product narrative or ad hook, read one industry-adjacent and one completely unrelated publication or community, and mine them for a metaphor or angle you can justify with your real product facts.","Make the borrowed angle serve the product truth, not replace it — a clever reference that overstates the product breaks believability."],"caveats":["The 30% hit rate is the source's own estimate from practice.","Borrowed metaphors must be checked against what your product actually does before use in claims."],"tags":["creative-strategy","copywriting","content","product-page","ad-creative","research"]}]}

Structuring creative tasks using an "approximate thinking" spectrum: encouraging teams to generate ideas that fall between "bizarre/absurd" and "safe/workable," explicitly asking them to stop at the "approximate" stage so ideas can be evaluated before they are fully baked or discarded.
